summary: Argues that pervasive monitoring is a technical attack that should be mitigated in the design of IETF protocols where possible. It is a Best Current Practice statement of IETF consensus.

eli5.summary: Someone secretly watching everyone's messages all the time is attacking the network. The people who design internet rules agree they should build protocols to make that harder.

questions: does the ietf require a pervasive monitoring section
subtitle: The IETF declares large-scale surveillance a technical attack and commits to designing protocols that make it harder.

tldr.problem: Widespread, often covert surveillance of Internet traffic and metadata threatens the privacy of users and organisations, and IETF standards generally did not address it.
tldr.mechanism: The IETF community records its consensus that pervasive monitoring is an attack in the technical sense, and that protocols should be designed to mitigate it where possible by making it significantly more expensive or infeasible.
tldr.outcome: Protocol authors must be able to say whether pervasive monitoring is relevant to their work and how they considered it. The RFC does not prescribe specific techniques, and it is a Best Current Practice that has not been obsoleted.

facts.label: Required new section
facts.value: None; authors only need a good answer if asked

today: RFC 7258 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 188) and has not been obsoleted or updated by another RFC. It records the IETF's consensus position that pervasive monitoring is an attack to be mitigated in protocol design where possible.

sections.title: What Pervasive Monitoring Is
sections.content:
Pervasive Monitoring (PM) is widespread, and often covert, surveillance through intrusive gathering of protocol artefacts. Those artefacts include application content and protocol metadata such as headers.

The RFC lists techniques that can be part of PM: active or passive wiretaps, traffic analysis (for example correlation, timing or measuring packet sizes), and subverting the cryptographic keys used to secure protocols. PM is distinguished by being indiscriminate and very large scale, rather than by introducing new types of technical compromise.

The IETF community's technical assessment is that PM is an attack on the privacy of Internet users and organisations. The topic was discussed at the technical plenary of the November 2013 IETF meeting and then through extensive exchanges on IETF mailing lists. This document records the resulting consensus.
sections.eli5: Pervasive monitoring means watching nearly everybody's messages, usually in secret. It is like a person who listens at every door in the street, not just one.

sections.title: Attack in a Technical Sense
sections.content:
The RFC says that it uses the word attack differently from everyday English. In common usage an attack is an aggressive action by an opponent. Here it means behavior that subverts the intent of communicating parties without their agreement. An attack may change the content of a communication, record its content or external characteristics, or reveal information through correlation with other communication events. RFC 4949 has a more complete definition.

Used technically, the word says nothing about the motivation of the attacker. Motivation for PM can range from non-targeted nation-state surveillance, to legal but privacy-unfriendly purposes by commercial enterprises, to illegal actions by criminals.

Because the same techniques are used whatever the motivation, the RFC argues that the IETF cannot defend against the most nefarious actors while allowing monitoring by others, however benevolent some might consider them. The motivation for PM is therefore not relevant to how it is mitigated in IETF protocols.
sections.eli5: In this document, an attack just means doing something to people's messages that they did not agree to. It does not matter whether the watcher thinks they are a good guy, because the sneaky listening looks the same either way.

sections.title: What the IETF Commits To
sections.content:
The RFC says that mitigation is a technical term and does not mean completely preventing an attack. Protocols that mitigate PM do not stop it, but they can significantly change the threat. They can increase the cost of attacking, force what was covert to be overt, or make the attack more likely to be detected, possibly later.

IETF standards already protect Internet communications, and RFC 3552 gives guidelines for applying them. The RFC observes that those standards generally do not address PM, the confidentiality of protocol metadata, countering traffic analysis, or data minimisation. The IETF will work to mitigate the technical aspects of PM, just as it does for protocol vulnerabilities in general. The specific ways will change over time and are not described in the RFC.

Specification authors need to be able to answer one question if asked: is pervasive monitoring relevant to this work, and if so, how has it been considered? This does not mean a new pervasive monitoring considerations section is required. Architectural decisions, including which existing technology is reused, may significantly affect a protocol's vulnerability to PM. Early review of those decisions matters because revisiting them late is very costly.
sections.eli5: The rule-writers promise to think about snoopers whenever they design something new. They cannot make snooping impossible, but they can make it cost more or easier to spot.

sections.title: Monitoring That Is Not an Attack
sections.content:
Not all monitoring is bad. The RFC gives network management functions that monitor packets or flows, and anti-spam mechanisms that need to see mail content, as examples of monitoring that can be beneficial. Some monitoring can even help mitigate PM: certificate transparency (RFC 6962) monitors Public Key Infrastructure in ways that could detect some PM attack techniques.

There is still clear potential for monitoring mechanisms to be abused for PM, so this tension needs careful consideration in protocol design. The RFC states that making networks unmanageable to mitigate PM is not an acceptable outcome, but that ignoring PM would go against the consensus documented here. It expects an appropriate balance to emerge over time as real instances are considered.
sections.eli5: A lifeguard watching the pool is helpful, and a stranger secretly filming it is not. The rule-writers want to stop the second kind without getting rid of the first.

sections.title: Limits of the IETF's Role
sections.content:
The IETF, as a standards development organisation, does not control the implementation or deployment of its specifications, although IETF participants do develop many implementations. It also does not standardise all layers of the protocol stack.

The non-technical aspects of mitigating pervasive monitoring, such as legal and political ones, are outside the scope of the IETF. The RFC concludes that the broader Internet community will need to step forward if PM is to be fully addressed.

Its own summary is: current capabilities permit some actors to monitor content and metadata across the Internet at a scale never before seen, this is an attack on Internet privacy, and the IETF will strive to produce specifications that mitigate it.
sections.eli5: The rule-writers can only fix the rules of the internet. Laws and politics belong to other people, so everyone has to help.

sections.title: Process Note
sections.content:
Earlier architectural statements of this kind, such as RFC 1984 and RFC 2804, were published as joint products of the IESG and the IAB. Since then the IETF and IAB have separated their publication streams, as described in RFC 4844 and RFC 5741.

This document was initiated after discussions in both the IESG and the IAB. It is published as an IETF-stream consensus document so that it properly reflects the consensus of the IETF community as a whole.
sections.eli5: Past statements like this came from two small groups of leaders. This one was published as the view of the whole community instead.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC says that the document is entirely about privacy. It points to RFC 6973 for the relationship between security and privacy threats, and notes that Section 5.1.1 of that RFC specifically treats surveillance as a combined security-privacy threat.
sections.eli5: This whole document is about keeping people's private things private, so there is not much more to add.
